description: Build a rare skill stack using the Scott Adams model: become top 25% at 3 things whose combination is held by very few people, then practice the weakest skill deliberately until the stack is balanced.

steps.description: Inventory every skill you use in your work and life, then estimate your percentile in each one relative to the general population.

inputs.name: work-description
inputs.desc: What you do for work and what you do outside work

inputs.name: skill-self-assessment
inputs.desc: Your honest sense of what you are good at and what you are not

outputs.name: skill-inventory
outputs.desc: Complete list of skills with estimated percentile for each

outputs.name: top-quartile-skills
outputs.desc: Skills where you are at or above the 75th percentile

process: List every skill you use regularly: technical skills, communication skills, domain knowledge, interpersonal skills, creative skills, analytical skills.
For each skill, estimate your percentile relative to the general working population. Use concrete evidence: formal training, years of practice, feedback received, output quality compared to peers.
Flag any skill where you are above the 75th percentile. These are your stack candidates.
Flag any skill where you are below the 25th percentile but wish you were better. These are potential growth targets.

steps.description: Score every possible 3-skill combination from your top-quartile skills by how rare that combination is in the population.

inputs.name: top-quartile-skills
inputs.desc: Skills where you are at or above the 75th percentile

outputs.name: combination-scores
outputs.desc: Every 3-skill combination ranked by rarity (fewer people hold all three at 75th+)

outputs.name: market-value-notes
outputs.desc: For the top 5 combinations, notes on where that combination is valuable

process: Generate every possible 3-skill combination from your top-quartile list.
For each combination, estimate how many people hold all three at the 75th percentile or above. The fewer people, the higher the rarity score.
Consider adjacency: skills from the same domain (two programming languages) are less rare together than skills from different domains (programming + sales + writing).
For the top 5 rarest combinations, identify specific roles, industries, or situations where that exact combination is disproportionately valuable.

steps.description: Choose your target skill stack by weighing rarity against market value and personal interest.

inputs.name: market-value-notes
inputs.desc: Where each top combination is valuable

outputs.name: chosen-stack
outputs.desc: The 3 skills you will build your identity around

outputs.name: stack-rationale
outputs.desc: Why this combination is rare, valuable, and worth your time

process: Eliminate any combination where one of the skills bores you. You will not sustain practice in something you find tedious.
Rank the remaining combinations by: rarity times market value times personal interest. All three matter.
Select the top combination. If two are close, pick the one where you have the most headroom for improvement (the weakest skill has the most upside).
Write one paragraph explaining why this stack is rare, where it is valuable, and what you will be able to do that most people cannot.

steps.description: Identify which of the three skills in your stack is currently weakest by measuring output quality, not self-perception.

inputs.name: chosen-stack
inputs.desc: The 3 skills in your target stack

outputs.name: weakest-skill
outputs.desc: The skill that needs the most improvement to balance the stack

outputs.name: gap-analysis
outputs.desc: Specific sub-skills or areas within the weakest skill where you fall short

process: For each of the three skills, gather evidence of your current output quality: recent work samples, peer feedback, test results, or competition benchmarks.
Compare your evidence against people who are solidly in the 75th percentile for that skill. Where do you fall short?
The weakest skill is the one with the largest gap between your current level and the 75th percentile. If all three are above 75th, the weakest is the one closest to dropping below.
Within the weakest skill, list the specific sub-skills or knowledge areas where you are deficient. These become your practice targets.

steps.description: Build a 90-day practice plan for the weakest skill, using deliberate practice principles rather than generic study.

inputs.name: gap-analysis
inputs.desc: Specific sub-skills where you fall short

outputs.name: practice-plan
outputs.desc: 90-day plan with weekly targets, specific drills, and feedback mechanisms

outputs.name: progress-milestones
outputs.desc: Measurable checkpoints at 30, 60, and 90 days

process: For each deficient sub-skill, design a drill that isolates that sub-skill and provides immediate feedback on performance.
Schedule practice sessions: minimum 3 times per week, 30-60 minutes each, focused on one sub-skill per session.
Set measurable milestones at 30, 60, and 90 days. Milestones should be output-based (produced X quality of work) not input-based (studied for Y hours).
Identify a feedback source for each sub-skill: a mentor, a peer, a test, a portfolio review, or a measurable metric.

steps.description: After the 90-day practice period, reassess all three skills and determine whether the stack is balanced or needs another round.

inputs.name: progress-milestones
inputs.desc: The checkpoints and whether they were met

outputs.name: updated-percentiles
outputs.desc: New percentile estimates for all three skills after practice

outputs.name: next-action
outputs.desc: Either the stack is balanced (all 3 at 75th+) or a new weakest skill needs a practice round

process: Reassess the practiced skill using the same evidence-based method: recent output quality, peer comparison, test results.
Reassess the other two skills as well. Sometimes neglecting them for 90 days causes slippage.
If all three are at or above the 75th percentile, the stack is balanced. Shift to maintenance mode: practice each skill at least once per week to prevent decay.
If one skill is still below 75th, it becomes the next practice target. Repeat the cycle.

description: Design a deliberate practice program for any skill: identify the weakest sub-skill through performance analysis, design drills that isolate it, practice at the edge of ability with immediate feedback, and shift targets as sub-skills improve.

steps.description: Break the target skill into its component sub-skills and measure your current performance in each one separately.

inputs.name: target-skill
inputs.desc: The skill you want to improve

inputs.name: current-performance-evidence
inputs.desc: Recent examples of your performance in this skill (recordings, work samples, scores, feedback)

outputs.name: sub-skill-map
outputs.desc: The target skill broken into 5-10 measurable sub-skills

outputs.name: sub-skill-scores
outputs.desc: Your current performance level in each sub-skill based on evidence, not self-assessment

process: Study how experts decompose this skill. Every complex skill is a bundle of smaller skills. A surgeon's skill includes hand steadiness, spatial reasoning, anatomical knowledge, decision-making under pressure, and communication with the team.
List 5-10 sub-skills for your target skill. Exclude any that are really the same skill described differently.
Score each sub-skill using your performance evidence. Watch recordings, review output, or ask someone who has observed you to rate each sub-skill independently.
Rank the sub-skills from weakest to strongest. The weakest one is your first practice target.

steps.description: Design a drill that isolates the weakest sub-skill so you can practice it without the other sub-skills masking or compensating.

inputs.name: sub-skill-map
inputs.desc: All sub-skills of the target skill

outputs.name: isolation-drill
outputs.desc: A specific exercise that targets the weakest sub-skill in isolation

outputs.name: difficulty-calibration
outputs.desc: How to set the drill difficulty so it is at the edge of your ability (not too easy, not too hard)

process: Take the weakest sub-skill and design an exercise that requires only that sub-skill. Remove or simplify everything else. If the sub-skill is 'transition between ideas in writing,' the drill is writing only transitions, not full essays.
Set the difficulty at the point where you succeed about 60-80% of the time. Below 60% is frustrating. Above 80% is too easy. Adjust by changing speed, complexity, or constraints.
Define what 'one rep' looks like. Each rep should take 1-5 minutes so you get many reps per session.
Define what success and failure look like for each rep. This must be objective enough that you can score yourself immediately.

steps.description: Set up an immediate feedback mechanism so you know after every rep whether you succeeded or failed and why.

inputs.name: difficulty-calibration
inputs.desc: How to set the challenge level

outputs.name: feedback-mechanism
outputs.desc: How you will get immediate feedback on each rep (self-scoring, recording review, coach observation, automated test)

outputs.name: tracking-method
outputs.desc: How you will track success rate over time to detect improvement or stagnation

process: Identify the fastest feedback mechanism available. In order of speed: real-time automated feedback (a test, a score), self-review of a recording immediately after, coach or peer observation, delayed review of output.
If no immediate feedback is available, create a rubric with 3-5 criteria you can score yourself on within 30 seconds of completing a rep.
Set up a tracking system: a simple spreadsheet or notebook where you log the date, number of reps, success rate, and any notes on what went wrong.
Plan to review your tracking data weekly to spot trends: improving, plateauing, or declining.

steps.description: Define the exact protocol for each practice session: warm-up, focused reps, cool-down review.

outputs.name: session-protocol
outputs.desc: Step-by-step instructions for running one practice session (30-60 minutes)

outputs.name: session-frequency
outputs.desc: How many sessions per week and when, scheduled into the calendar

process: Warm-up (5 minutes): do 3-5 reps at an easier difficulty to activate the sub-skill without fatigue.

Focused practice (20-40 minutes): do reps at the calibrated difficulty. After each rep, score it immediately. After every 5 reps, review what went wrong on the failures and adjust your approach for the next 5.

Cool-down review (5-10 minutes): log the session data (total reps, success rate, difficulty level). Write one sentence about the most common failure pattern. Write one sentence about what you will try differently next session.
Schedule 3-5 sessions per week. Deliberate practice is mentally taxing, so sessions beyond 60 minutes produce diminishing returns.

steps.description: Define when and how to increase drill difficulty as you improve, so practice stays at the edge of ability.

outputs.name: progression-rules
outputs.desc: When to increase difficulty (success rate threshold), how to increase it (specific levers), and when to decrease it (frustration threshold)

outputs.name: difficulty-levers
outputs.desc: The specific dimensions you can adjust: speed, complexity, constraints, time pressure

process: Increase difficulty when your success rate exceeds 80% for three consecutive sessions. You have learned this level; staying here is repetition, not practice.
Decrease difficulty if your success rate drops below 50% for two consecutive sessions. You jumped too far; back off one increment.

Identify the specific levers for your drill. For writing: increase word count constraints, add a new audience, reduce revision time. For a physical skill: increase speed, reduce rest between reps, add an obstacle.
When you increase difficulty, expect your success rate to drop to 60-70%. This is correct. If it does not drop, you did not increase enough.

steps.description: Define when to stop practicing the current sub-skill and rotate to the next weakest one.

outputs.name: rotation-criteria
outputs.desc: The specific conditions under which you stop practicing this sub-skill and move to the next

outputs.name: reassessment-protocol
outputs.desc: How to re-score all sub-skills to find the new weakest

process: Rotate when the current sub-skill is no longer the weakest. This typically happens when you can perform at the target level consistently (80%+ success rate at the target difficulty for 5 consecutive sessions).
To find the new weakest: re-perform the original performance decomposition. Your sub-skill scores have shifted. The new weakest gets the next practice cycle.
Do not rotate too early. A sub-skill that feels improved but has not been tested at the target difficulty is not actually improved.
Maintain each improved sub-skill with one session per week to prevent decay while you focus on the new target.

description: Build a spaced repetition system that fights the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: schedule reviews at increasing intervals (1, 3, 7, 14, 30, 90 days), reset intervals on failure, and produce better retention from fewer total reviews than massed study.

steps.description: Extract discrete, testable knowledge items from the material you need to retain.

inputs.name: source-material
inputs.desc: The content you need to learn and retain (textbook, notes, course material, procedures)

inputs.name: retention-goal
inputs.desc: What you need to be able to do with this knowledge (recall facts, apply procedures, recognize patterns)

outputs.name: knowledge-items
outputs.desc: A list of discrete, testable items: each one is a single fact, concept, procedure step, or association

outputs.name: item-format-map
outputs.desc: For each item, the test format that best measures retention (recall, recognition, application, explanation)

process: Read through the source material and identify each discrete piece of knowledge that you need to retain. A discrete item is one that can be tested with a single question.
Avoid items that are too broad ('explain cardiac physiology') or too trivial ('the heart has chambers'). Aim for items you could test in 10-30 seconds.

For each item, choose the test format that matches your retention goal. If you need to recall under pressure, use free recall. If you need to recognize patterns, use recognition. If you need to apply, use scenario-based questions.
Group related items so you can review them in clusters, but test each item independently.

steps.description: Create review cards (questions and answers) for each knowledge item, using the minimum information principle: one item per card.

inputs.name: item-format-map
inputs.desc: The test format for each item

outputs.name: review-cards
outputs.desc: A set of cards, each with a prompt (question) and a response (answer), one item per card

outputs.name: card-count
outputs.desc: Total number of cards created

process: Write one card per knowledge item. The prompt should trigger recall of exactly one piece of knowledge. If you need two pieces of knowledge to answer, split it into two cards.
Make prompts specific and unambiguous. 'What is the half-life of caffeine?' is better than 'Tell me about caffeine.'
For application items, write the prompt as a scenario: 'A patient presents with X, Y, Z. What is the next diagnostic step?'
Include a brief source reference on each card so you can look up the context if the answer surprises you during review.

steps.description: Configure the review intervals based on the Ebbinghaus curve: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days, 30 days, 90 days after initial learning.

outputs.name: interval-schedule
outputs.desc: The review schedule: each card starts at interval 1 (1 day), and advances through 3, 7, 14, 30, 90 days on each successful review

outputs.name: daily-review-estimate
outputs.desc: Estimated number of cards to review per day once the system reaches steady state

process: Assign every new card to interval 0 (review tomorrow, 1 day after first seeing it).
On successful recall, advance the card to the next interval: 1 day to 3 days to 7 days to 14 days to 30 days to 90 days.
On failed recall, reset the card to interval 0 (review again tomorrow). This is the critical rule: failure resets the clock because the memory trace has decayed.
Estimate steady-state daily load: with N total cards and a 90% success rate, expect to review roughly N/5 cards per day once the system stabilizes.

steps.description: Run a daily review session: present each due card, test recall, score pass/fail, and update the interval.

inputs.name: interval-schedule
inputs.desc: The current schedule with due dates for each card

outputs.name: session-results
outputs.desc: For each reviewed card: pass or fail, time to answer, and the new interval

outputs.name: updated-schedule
outputs.desc: The schedule with updated due dates based on today's results

process: Pull all cards due today (due date is today or earlier).
For each card: read the prompt, attempt to recall the answer before looking, then check your answer. Score it pass (recalled correctly and completely) or fail (any error or blank).
Be strict on scoring. A partial answer is a fail. The point of the system is to build reliable recall, and lenient scoring undermines it.
Update each card's interval and due date based on the score. A pass advances to the next interval. A fail resets to interval 0.

steps.description: Analyze retention patterns to identify problem cards (leeches) and adjust the system.

outputs.name: leech-cards
outputs.desc: Cards that have been reset 3 or more times (they are not sticking and need a different approach)

outputs.name: retention-rate
outputs.desc: Overall pass rate across all reviews, broken down by interval level

process: Identify leech cards: any card reset to interval 0 three or more times. These items are not sticking with simple repetition.

For leech cards, rewrite the card. Common fixes: make the prompt more specific, add a mnemonic or visual association, split a complex item into smaller items, or connect it to something you already know well.
Calculate retention rate by interval level. If retention drops below 85% at a specific interval (say the 14-day to 30-day jump), consider adding an intermediate interval (21 days).
Review monthly: if the daily load is too high, you may be adding new cards too fast. Limit new cards to 10-20 per day until the backlog clears.

steps.description: Periodically test whether spaced repetition is producing usable knowledge, not just card-passing ability.

outputs.name: integration-test-results
outputs.desc: Performance on an open-ended task that requires combining multiple knowledge items

outputs.name: system-adjustments
outputs.desc: Changes to make: add application cards, group related items, or retire well-known items

process: Design an open-ended test that requires combining multiple knowledge items to solve a problem. This tests whether you can USE the knowledge, not just recall isolated facts.
Take the test without looking at your cards. Score yourself honestly.
If you can recall individual cards but cannot combine them, add 'connection cards' that explicitly link related items (e.g., 'How does X relate to Y?').
Retire cards for items that have reached the 90-day interval and been passed three times at that level. They are in long-term memory.

description: Build a personal library of mental models, starting with the 10 most broadly useful, and practice applying each one to real decisions until model selection becomes automatic.

steps.description: Learn the precise definition of each of the 10 core mental models: first principles, inversion, second-order thinking, Pareto principle, opportunity cost, margin of safety, feedback loops, compounding, reversion to mean, map is not territory.

inputs.name: current-decision-domain
inputs.desc: The domain where you make most of your decisions (business, engineering, personal, investing, management)

inputs.name: known-models
inputs.desc: Mental models you already use, even informally

outputs.name: model-definitions
outputs.desc: Precise one-paragraph definition of each of the 10 core models, with the key question each one answers

outputs.name: model-trigger-conditions
outputs.desc: For each model, the situation type where it is most useful (e.g., inversion is most useful when you are stuck on 'how to succeed' and should instead ask 'how would I guarantee failure')

process: For each model, write a one-paragraph definition in your own words (not copied). If you cannot explain it simply, you do not understand it yet.

For each model, write the key question it answers. First principles: 'What is actually true here, independent of convention?' Inversion: 'What would guarantee failure, and am I doing any of those things?' Second-order: 'And then what?'
For each model, identify the trigger condition: the type of situation where this model produces the most insight.
Identify which models you already use informally. You probably use 2-3 without naming them. The goal is to add the other 7-8 deliberately.

steps.description: For each mental model, find 3 examples from your own past decisions where that model would have been useful (whether or not you used it at the time).

inputs.name: model-definitions
inputs.desc: The 10 model definitions and trigger conditions

outputs.name: example-library
outputs.desc: 3 examples per model (30 total) drawn from your own experience, each showing what the model reveals about that decision

outputs.name: missed-insight-notes
outputs.desc: For each example where you did NOT use the model at the time, what you would have done differently

process: For each model, review your recent decisions (past 6-12 months) and find 3 where the model applies. At least 1 should be a decision where you did not use the model and it would have changed your choice.
For each example, write: (1) the decision, (2) what the model reveals when applied, (3) whether you used the model at the time, (4) what you would have done differently.
If you cannot find 3 examples for a model, the model may not be relevant to your domain. Replace it with one that is. The 10 core models are starting points, not sacred.
The purpose of personal examples is to anchor abstract models to concrete memories. Abstract definitions fade; personal stories stick.

steps.description: Set up a weekly practice routine: apply one model deliberately to a real decision each week and record what it revealed.

outputs.name: weekly-practice-schedule
outputs.desc: A 10-week rotation assigning one model per week, with instructions for applying it to a real decision that week

outputs.name: application-log-template
outputs.desc: A template for recording each week's application: the decision, the model, what it revealed, whether it changed your choice

process: Assign one model per week for a 10-week cycle. Start with the model you are least familiar with (it needs the most practice).
Each week, identify at least one real decision (not hypothetical) to apply the model to. Apply the model by asking its key question and writing down the answer before making the decision.
After the decision is made (or the week ends), record: what the model revealed, whether it changed your thinking, and whether the outcome validated or contradicted the model's insight.
After 10 weeks, you will have applied each model at least once. The ones that produced the most insight for your domain become your core toolkit.

steps.description: After one full cycle, rank the models by how much insight they produced in your specific domain and situation.

inputs.name: application-log-template
inputs.desc: The log template (now filled with 10 weeks of data)

outputs.name: model-rankings
outputs.desc: The 10 models ranked by insight produced in your domain, with evidence from the application log

outputs.name: top-5-models
outputs.desc: Your personal top 5 models, the ones you should apply most frequently

process: Review your 10 weeks of application logs. For each model, count: how many times it changed your thinking, how many times the outcome validated its insight, how easy it was to apply.
Rank the models by impact. The models that changed your thinking AND were validated by outcomes rank highest.
Your top 5 become your default toolkit. When facing a decision, run through these 5 before choosing. The other 5 remain available for situations that match their trigger conditions.

If any model produced zero insight across the cycle, replace it with a model from outside the core 10 that might fit your domain better (e.g., Bayesian updating for data-heavy domains, theory of constraints for operations).

steps.description: Practice combining two or more models on a single decision to produce deeper insight than any one model alone.

outputs.name: combination-patterns
outputs.desc: 2-3 model combinations that work well together in your domain (e.g., inversion + second-order thinking for risk analysis)

outputs.name: combination-practice-plan
outputs.desc: A plan for applying model combinations to upcoming decisions

process: Take a complex upcoming decision and apply your top 5 models to it sequentially. Note where one model's output becomes another model's input.

Identify natural pairings: inversion + second-order thinking (what would fail, and then what?), Pareto + opportunity cost (which 20% matters most, and what am I giving up?), first principles + margin of safety (what is true, and how much buffer do I need?).
Record 2-3 combinations that produced richer insight together than either model alone. These become your multi-model workflows for complex decisions.
Practice applying these combinations to one complex decision per month. The goal is for model selection and combination to become automatic, not effortful.

steps.description: Expand your model library beyond the core 10 by adding domain-specific models and retiring models that do not fit.

inputs.name: model-rankings
inputs.desc: Rankings showing which models work and which do not

inputs.name: combination-patterns
inputs.desc: Model combinations that work in your domain

outputs.name: expanded-library
outputs.desc: Your personalized model library (10-15 models) with definitions, trigger conditions, and personal examples for each

outputs.name: maintenance-plan
outputs.desc: How to keep the library current: add new models when encountered, retire models that stop producing insight, and review quarterly

process: Retire any model that produced zero insight after two full cycles. Replace it with a domain-specific model: theory of constraints (operations), Bayesian updating (data analysis), comparative advantage (career), network effects (technology), loss aversion (sales and negotiation).
For each new model, go through the same process: define it, find 3 personal examples, apply it for one week, and score its usefulness.
Cap the library at 15 models. A library too large is unused. The constraint forces you to keep only the models that actually change your decisions.
Review the library quarterly. Remove any model you have not applied in 3 months. Add any model you found yourself needing but did not have.

description: Redesign the physical and digital environment so the desired behavior is the default and the undesired behavior requires effort, using the principle that behavior is a function of environment more than willpower.

steps.description: Define the specific behaviors you want to increase and the specific behaviors you want to decrease, stated as observable actions, not aspirations.

inputs.name: desired-outcomes
inputs.desc: What you want to achieve (health, productivity, learning, financial, relationship goals)

inputs.name: current-struggles
inputs.desc: What you currently struggle to do or struggle to stop doing

outputs.name: increase-behaviors
outputs.desc: 3-5 specific behaviors you want to do more often, stated as observable actions with frequency targets

outputs.name: decrease-behaviors
outputs.desc: 3-5 specific behaviors you want to do less often, stated as observable actions with reduction targets

process: Convert each desired outcome into a specific, observable behavior. 'Be healthier' becomes 'eat a vegetable with every meal' and 'walk 30 minutes daily.' The behavior must be something a camera could record.
Convert each struggle into a specific behavior to decrease. 'Stop wasting time' becomes 'open social media fewer than 3 times per day.'
Set a frequency target for each behavior. Increase behaviors need a minimum (at least X times per week). Decrease behaviors need a maximum (no more than X times per week).
Limit to 3-5 in each category. Environment redesign works best when focused. Trying to change 15 behaviors simultaneously changes none.

steps.description: Audit the current environment for cues that trigger each behavior (both desired and undesired), mapping the physical and digital triggers.

outputs.name: cue-map
outputs.desc: For each behavior, the specific environmental cues that trigger it: what you see, hear, or encounter that leads to the behavior

outputs.name: friction-assessment
outputs.desc: For each behavior, how many steps it takes to start (the friction level)

process: For each undesired behavior, track when and where it happens for 3 days. What preceded it? What did you see, hear, or feel right before? The cue is usually visual (you saw the phone, the snack, the tab).

For each desired behavior, identify what currently prevents you from doing it. How many steps does it take to start? Where is the friction? If going to the gym requires packing a bag, driving, parking, and changing, that is 4 friction points.

Map the physical environment: where objects are placed, what is visible, what is within arm's reach. Map the digital environment: what apps are on the home screen, what notifications are on, what tabs are open.
The cue audit reveals that most behaviors are triggered by the environment, not by conscious choice. This is why willpower fails: you are fighting the environment dozens of times per day.

steps.description: Add friction to undesired behaviors and remove friction from desired behaviors by changing the environment.

inputs.name: friction-assessment
inputs.desc: Current friction levels for each behavior

outputs.name: friction-changes
outputs.desc: Specific changes to make: items to move, apps to rearrange, defaults to change, obstacles to add or remove

outputs.name: implementation-checklist
outputs.desc: A checklist of physical and digital changes to make in one session

process: For each desired behavior, reduce friction to one step or zero steps. Lay out workout clothes the night before (zero-step start). Put the book on the pillow (you see it when you get into bed). Put the healthy food at eye level in the fridge.

For each undesired behavior, add friction. Delete social media apps from the phone (you can still use them in a browser, but the extra steps reduce impulse use). Move snacks to a high shelf in a closed cabinet. Log out of streaming services after each use.

Change defaults. The default should be the desired behavior. If the TV is off by default and requires 3 steps to start, you will watch less. If the meditation app opens when you unlock your phone in the morning, you will meditate more.
Make the changes all at once. A gradual rollout lets the old cues persist. Clear the environment in one session.

steps.description: Redesign the social environment: surround yourself with people who model the desired behavior and reduce exposure to people who model the undesired behavior.

outputs.name: social-changes
outputs.desc: Specific changes to social environment: groups to join, people to spend more time with, contexts to avoid

outputs.name: accountability-setup
outputs.desc: One accountability partner or group for the most important behavior change

process: Identify people in your life who already do the behavior you want to adopt. Spend more time with them in the context where they do that behavior. You absorb behavior from your social environment without conscious effort.

Identify contexts where the undesired behavior is the social norm. You do not need to cut off friendships, but you may need to change the context (meet at a coffee shop instead of a bar if you are reducing alcohol).

Find or create one accountability setup: a partner, a group, or a public commitment. The mechanism is simple: tell someone what you intend to do and agree to report back. The social pressure adds friction to skipping.
The social environment is the most powerful and most overlooked design lever. A person who joins a running group runs more than a person who buys running shoes.

steps.description: Review the redesigned environment after 2 weeks and again after 6 weeks to check whether the behavior change is holding.

outputs.name: behavior-tracking-results
outputs.desc: Actual frequency of each target behavior over the review period compared to the target

outputs.name: environment-adjustments
outputs.desc: Changes that worked (keep), changes that did not work (modify), and new friction points discovered (address)

process: Track each target behavior daily for the review period. Use a simple tally: did the behavior happen today (yes/no/how many times)?

At the 2-week mark, compare actual frequency to target. Behaviors where the environment change worked (within 20% of target) need no adjustment. Behaviors that did not change need a different environmental intervention.
For behaviors that did not change, look for cues you missed in the original audit. There is usually a trigger you did not remove or a friction point you did not add.
At the 6-week mark, the behaviors that held through 6 weeks are becoming habits. Shift attention to the ones that are still struggling. The environment may need a more aggressive redesign.

description: Find the ONE habit that cascades into others: the keystone habit where adopting it causes positive spillover into other behaviors without additional effort, because it sits upstream in the causal chain.

steps.description: List every behavior change you want to make, without filtering or prioritizing yet.

inputs.name: life-areas
inputs.desc: The areas of life you want to improve (health, work, relationships, finance, learning, creativity)

inputs.name: frustrations
inputs.desc: Specific things you are frustrated about or wish were different

outputs.name: change-list
outputs.desc: Complete list of 10-20 behavior changes you want to make, stated as specific actions

outputs.name: importance-ratings
outputs.desc: Each change rated by how much it would improve your life if adopted (1-10)

process: List every behavior you wish you did more of or less of. Do not filter. Include small changes (drink more water) and large ones (exercise daily). Include habits you have tried and failed to adopt.
State each change as a specific action, not an aspiration. 'Exercise 4 times per week' not 'be healthier.'
Rate each change by importance: how much would your life improve if this change stuck? Use a 1-10 scale where 10 means it would change everything.
Do not prioritize yet. The goal is a complete inventory, not a plan.

steps.description: Map the causal connections between the behavior changes: which ones cause or enable others.

outputs.name: causal-map
outputs.desc: A directed graph showing which behaviors cause or enable other behaviors (A leads to B means adopting A makes B easier or more likely)

outputs.name: upstream-counts
outputs.desc: For each behavior, how many other behaviors it sits upstream of (directly or indirectly)

process: For each pair of behaviors on the list, ask: does adopting behavior A make behavior B easier, more likely, or automatic? If yes, draw an arrow from A to B.

Example: 'exercise daily' leads to 'sleep better' (exercise improves sleep quality), which leads to 'wake up earlier' (better sleep means easier mornings), which leads to 'have a morning routine' (waking earlier creates time).
Count the upstream connections for each behavior. A behavior with 5 downstream connections is more upstream than one with 1.
Look for behaviors that appear upstream of multiple independent chains. These are keystone habit candidates.

steps.description: Score each keystone candidate by: number of downstream behaviors, your current ability to adopt it, and whether it has a natural feedback loop.

inputs.name: causal-map
inputs.desc: The directed graph of behavior connections

inputs.name: upstream-counts
inputs.desc: How many behaviors each one sits upstream of

outputs.name: keystone-scores
outputs.desc: Each candidate scored on three dimensions: downstream impact, adoptability, and feedback loop strength

outputs.name: top-keystone
outputs.desc: The single best keystone habit candidate with the rationale for choosing it

process: Score downstream impact (1-10): how many other behaviors does this one cascade into? The more, the higher the score.
Score adoptability (1-10): how hard is this behavior to start? A behavior you have tried and failed 5 times scores low. A behavior that requires only a small environment change scores high.

Score feedback loop strength (1-10): does this behavior produce a noticeable reward quickly? Exercise produces endorphins within 30 minutes (strong loop). Saving money produces no immediate reward (weak loop).
Multiply the three scores. The highest total is your keystone habit. If two are close, pick the one with higher adoptability (you need to actually do it for the cascade to start).

steps.description: Build a focused plan to adopt the keystone habit using environment design and the minimum viable version.

outputs.name: adoption-plan
outputs.desc: A 30-day plan to establish the keystone habit, starting with the minimum viable version and scaling up

outputs.name: environment-changes
outputs.desc: Specific physical and digital environment changes to make the keystone habit the default

process: Define the minimum viable version of the keystone habit. If the habit is 'exercise 4 times per week,' the minimum viable version is 'put on workout clothes and stand outside for 5 minutes, 4 times per week.' The barrier must be so low that not doing it feels ridiculous.
Make the environment changes that reduce friction to zero. Lay out the clothes. Set the alarm. Block the calendar. Remove competing cues.
Plan the 30-day ramp: week 1 is the minimum viable version only. Week 2 adds 50% of the target. Week 3 adds 75%. Week 4 is the full target. This ramp builds the habit before increasing the effort.
Identify the first downstream behavior you expect to see change without deliberate effort. This is your confirmation signal that the cascade is working.

steps.description: After 30 days with the keystone habit, check whether the downstream behaviors actually changed without additional effort.

inputs.name: adoption-plan
inputs.desc: The keystone habit plan that was executed

outputs.name: cascade-results
outputs.desc: For each expected downstream behavior: did it actually improve, stay the same, or get worse?

outputs.name: next-action
outputs.desc: If the cascade is working, continue. If not, reassess whether the chosen habit is truly a keystone or whether the causal connections were wrong.

process: Track the downstream behaviors for the full 30-day period. Do not try to adopt them. The point of a keystone habit is that the downstream changes happen without additional willpower.
Compare: did the downstream behaviors actually change? If exercise was the keystone and you expected better sleep, did sleep actually improve?
If the cascade is working (2+ downstream behaviors improved), continue the keystone habit and let the cascade deepen over the next 60 days.

If the cascade did not materialize, one of two things happened: the keystone habit was not truly upstream (the causal map was wrong), or the keystone habit was not adopted firmly enough. Check which one.

description: Design a learning project that produces a tangible artifact AND the skill: learning by building is 5-10x more effective than learning by consuming, because building forces you to encounter the hard parts.

steps.description: Match the skill you want to learn to a project type that forces encounter with the hard parts of that skill.

inputs.name: target-skill
inputs.desc: The skill you want to learn or improve

inputs.name: current-level
inputs.desc: Your current level in this skill (beginner, intermediate, advanced)

outputs.name: project-candidates
outputs.desc: 3 project ideas that would teach this skill through building, ranked by how many hard sub-skills they force you to use

outputs.name: hard-parts-coverage
outputs.desc: For each project, which hard parts of the skill it covers and which it skips

process: List the hard parts of the skill. Every skill has parts that beginners avoid and experts know are essential. For coding: debugging, error handling, edge cases. For writing: structure, editing, concision. For design: constraints, user testing, iteration.
For each hard part, design a project that forces you to encounter it. The project must make it impossible to skip the hard parts by making them central to the deliverable.
Rank the project candidates by hard-part coverage. The project that covers the most hard parts is the best learning project, even if it is harder.
Eliminate projects where you could succeed without using the target skill (e.g., a 'coding' project where you mostly copy existing code).

steps.description: Scope the project to the stretch zone: slightly beyond your current skill level but not in the panic zone.

outputs.name: scoped-project
outputs.desc: The chosen project scoped to 2-4 weeks, with clear boundaries on what is in and out of scope

outputs.name: stretch-elements
outputs.desc: The specific aspects of the project that are beyond your current ability (these are where the learning happens)

process: The stretch zone is where you can succeed with effort but not with your current skills alone. If you could complete the project today with your current skills, it is too easy. If you have no idea where to start, it is too hard.
Scope to 2-4 weeks of part-time work (10-20 hours per week). Longer projects lose momentum. Shorter projects do not cover enough hard parts.

Define what is in scope (the specific deliverable) and out of scope (things that would be nice but are not necessary for the learning objective). Scope creep turns learning projects into never-finished projects.
Explicitly identify the 2-3 elements that are beyond your current ability. These are the learning targets. Everything else in the project is scaffolding.

steps.description: Break the project into milestones where each milestone produces a working (if incomplete) version and exercises at least one hard part.

inputs.name: scoped-project
inputs.desc: The chosen project with scope boundaries

outputs.name: milestone-plan
outputs.desc: 4-6 milestones, each producing a working version, each exercising at least one hard part of the skill

outputs.name: milestone-deliverables
outputs.desc: The specific, tangible output of each milestone that you can show to someone

process: Each milestone must produce something that works, even if it is rough. Milestone 1 should produce a working prototype in the first 3-5 days. Nothing kills learning faster than spending 3 weeks with nothing to show.
Order milestones so that the first milestone covers the most foundational hard part. If you fail at the foundation, you learn that early instead of late.
Each milestone after the first should add one hard part. By the final milestone, all stretch elements have been exercised.
Make each milestone's deliverable something you can share with another person for feedback. External feedback on a tangible artifact is the fastest way to calibrate your skill level.

steps.description: Build a just-in-time resource strategy: identify what you will need to learn at each milestone and where you will find it, but do not study it all upfront.

outputs.name: resource-map
outputs.desc: For each milestone, the 1-3 resources (tutorials, documentation, examples, people) you will consult when you hit the hard part

outputs.name: learning-triggers
outputs.desc: The specific moment in each milestone when you should stop building and start learning (the point where you are stuck, not the point where you are bored)

process: Do NOT study all the material before starting the project. Upfront study produces the illusion of preparation without the reality of skill. Study when you are stuck, not before.

For each milestone, identify the hard part and the 1-3 resources most likely to help when you encounter it. A good resource is specific (covers this exact topic), practical (shows examples), and concise (does not require 40 hours of reading).
Define the learning trigger: the moment when you have tried for 30 minutes and are genuinely stuck. That is when you consult the resource. Not before. The struggle is the learning.
If a resource does not help within 20 minutes, switch to a different resource or ask a person. Spending 3 hours on a bad tutorial is wasted practice time.

steps.description: After each milestone, get feedback from someone who can evaluate the output and integrate it before starting the next milestone.

outputs.name: feedback-plan
outputs.desc: Who will review each milestone, what you will ask them, and how you will integrate their feedback

outputs.name: quality-criteria
outputs.desc: For each milestone, the specific quality criteria that distinguish good output from adequate output

process: Identify one person for each milestone who can evaluate the output. This person should be better than you at the skill (they can spot errors you cannot see).
Ask specific questions, not 'what do you think?' Ask: 'Does this work correctly for edge case X?' or 'Where would a user get confused?' Specific questions produce specific feedback.

After receiving feedback, categorize it: critical (must fix before next milestone), important (should fix, improves quality), nice-to-have (optional). Fix all critical items. Address as many important items as time allows.
The feedback loop is the mechanism that converts building into learning. Without feedback, you practice your mistakes. With feedback, you correct them.

steps.description: After completing the project, assess what you actually learned and identify the next learning project.

outputs.name: skill-assessment
outputs.desc: Honest assessment of your current skill level after the project, compared to before, with specific evidence

outputs.name: next-project-direction
outputs.desc: The hard part you still need to work on, which becomes the seed for the next learning project

process: Compare your first milestone output to your final output. The difference is visible evidence of learning. If there is no visible difference, the project was too easy or you did not engage with the hard parts.
List what you learned that you did not expect to learn. The most valuable learning in a project is often not the planned learning but the unexpected discoveries.
Identify the hard part you still struggle with. This becomes the focus of your next learning project. Skill acquisition is iterative: each project reduces the gap but does not close it entirely.
Publish or share the final artifact. A shared artifact creates accountability and a public portfolio. The artifact is the proof.

description: Actively seek feedback that people will not volunteer: design specific asks, time them correctly, make them safe to answer honestly, and look for patterns across multiple sources.

steps.description: Identify the specific behavior or output you want feedback on, not a general request for opinions.

inputs.name: recent-performance
inputs.desc: A recent event, presentation, project, or interaction where you want to know how you did

inputs.name: self-assessment
inputs.desc: Your own sense of how it went and where you might be weak

outputs.name: feedback-targets
outputs.desc: 2-3 specific behaviors or outputs you want feedback on, each stated as a concrete observable thing

outputs.name: blind-spot-hypotheses
outputs.desc: Areas where you suspect you have blind spots (you think you are fine but might not be)

process: Convert 'how did I do' into 2-3 specific questions. 'How was my presentation' becomes 'Did I explain the pricing model clearly enough?' and 'Was the Q&A section too long?'
Include at least one question about a suspected blind spot. These are areas where your self-assessment might be wrong because you lack the external perspective to evaluate yourself.
Avoid questions that invite flattery ('Did you like it?') or are too broad ('Any feedback?'). Specific questions produce specific answers.
Frame each question so that an honest negative answer is as easy to give as a positive one. 'Was the timing right, or should I have cut 5 minutes?' makes it easy to say 'cut 5 minutes.'

steps.description: Choose 3 people who observed the behavior and who have different perspectives on it.

inputs.name: feedback-targets
inputs.desc: The specific things you want feedback on

outputs.name: feedback-sources
outputs.desc: 3 people to ask, each chosen for a different perspective (e.g., a peer, a direct report, a client or audience member)

outputs.name: source-rationale
outputs.desc: Why each person was chosen and what perspective they bring

process: Choose people who were actually present and paid attention. Second-hand feedback ('I heard it went well') is useless.

Choose from different vantage points. A peer, a subordinate, and a customer see different things. A peer notices technical quality. A subordinate notices communication clarity. A customer notices relevance.
Include at least one person who will be honest even if the feedback is negative. This is usually someone with high trust and no political reason to flatter you.
Avoid asking only people who will agree with your self-assessment. The value of feedback is in the delta between your perception and theirs.

steps.description: Design the ask so that giving honest negative feedback is safe and easy for the respondent.

outputs.name: ask-scripts
outputs.desc: The exact words you will use to ask each person, including the safety framing

outputs.name: timing-plan
outputs.desc: When to ask each person (ideally within 24-48 hours of the event)

process: Open with a frame that makes honesty easy: 'I am actively working on improving X, and I need honest feedback to do that. Sugarcoating it will not help me. Can you tell me [specific question]?'
Ask one question at a time. Multiple questions in one ask get averaged into one vague answer.
Time the ask within 24-48 hours of the event. After that, memory fades and the feedback becomes generic ('it was fine').

Ask in a private setting (one-on-one, not in a group). People will not give honest feedback in front of others. Written (text, email) can work if the person is uncomfortable giving negative feedback face-to-face.

steps.description: Receive the feedback without defensiveness, because how you receive feedback determines whether people give it to you in the future.

outputs.name: reception-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for receiving feedback: no defending, no explaining, no minimizing, just listen and ask follow-up questions

outputs.name: follow-up-questions
outputs.desc: Questions to ask when you need more specificity: 'Can you give me an example?' and 'What would you have done differently?'

process: When receiving feedback, your only job is to understand it. Do not defend, explain, or justify. The moment you defend, the person stops being honest.
Say 'thank you' after every piece of feedback, positive or negative. This signals that you value honesty and will not punish it.

Ask clarifying questions: 'Can you give me a specific example of when that happened?' and 'If you were in my position, what would you have done instead?' These turn vague feedback into actionable insight.
If a piece of feedback stings, that is usually a sign it is accurate. The feedback that does not sting is the feedback you already knew.

steps.description: Compare feedback from all 3 sources and look for the pattern, not the outlier.

outputs.name: feedback-patterns
outputs.desc: Themes that appeared in 2 or more responses (these are the real signals)

outputs.name: action-items
outputs.desc: 1-2 specific things to change based on the patterns, with a plan for when and how to practice the change

process: Lay out all three responses side by side. Look for themes that appear in 2 or more. A theme in 2 of 3 is a pattern. A theme in 1 of 3 is an opinion.
Ignore outlier feedback that contradicts the other two. One person's pet peeve is not a universal problem.
Convert each pattern into one specific action item. 'I talked too fast' becomes 'In the next presentation, pause for 2 seconds after each key point.' The action must be behavioral and observable.
Limit to 1-2 action items. Trying to change 5 things at once changes nothing. Pick the pattern with the highest impact and practice it until it is natural, then address the next one.

description: Transfer expertise from one person to another without losing the tacit knowledge, using the critical decision method: have the expert walk through real cases and extract the cues, meanings, and judgment calls that they cannot articulate in the abstract.

steps.description: Select the expert and frame the interview so they understand you are extracting tacit knowledge, not testing their ability.

inputs.name: expertise-domain
inputs.desc: The domain of expertise you want to transfer (medical diagnosis, negotiation, project estimation, debugging, sales, etc.)

inputs.name: expert-candidates
inputs.desc: People who have demonstrated expertise in this domain through consistent high performance

outputs.name: selected-expert
outputs.desc: The expert chosen for the interview, with the reason they were selected

outputs.name: interview-framing
outputs.desc: The explanation you will give the expert: what you are doing, why, and what kind of stories you need from them

process: Select an expert based on demonstrated performance, not title or tenure. The best expert is someone who consistently makes correct non-obvious decisions in ambiguous situations.

Frame the interview: 'I want to learn how you make decisions in [domain]. I am going to ask you to walk me through specific cases where you made a judgment call that turned out to be right. I am not testing you; I am trying to understand the thinking behind your decisions so I can learn from it.'
Schedule 60-90 minutes in a quiet setting. The interview requires concentration and memory retrieval, so avoid interruptions.
Prepare to record (with permission) or take detailed notes. The specific words the expert uses are important because they reveal their mental categories.

steps.description: Have the expert walk through 3-5 real cases where they made a non-obvious judgment call, using the critical decision method.

inputs.name: interview-framing
inputs.desc: How the interview was set up

outputs.name: case-narratives
outputs.desc: 3-5 detailed case narratives, each including the situation, the cues the expert noticed, the interpretation, the decision, and the outcome

outputs.name: decision-points
outputs.desc: The specific moments in each case where the expert's choice diverged from what a novice would have done

process: Ask: 'Think of a time when you made a decision in [domain] that turned out well, and that most people in your position would not have made. Walk me through what happened.'
As they tell the story, probe at each decision point: 'What did you notice at that moment?' 'What did that cue mean to you?' 'What options did you consider?' 'Why did you rule out the other options?'
Repeat for 3-5 cases. Choose cases of different types: a routine case with a hidden twist, a case where the expert overruled conventional wisdom, a case where time pressure forced a fast decision.
Do not judge or evaluate during the interview. Your job is to extract, not to assess. Ask 'what happened next?' not 'was that the right call?'

steps.description: Extract the tacit knowledge from the case narratives: the cues, patterns, and heuristics the expert uses but cannot articulate in the abstract.

inputs.name: decision-points
inputs.desc: The moments where the expert diverged from the obvious choice

outputs.name: cue-catalog
outputs.desc: The specific cues the expert noticed across cases (what they pay attention to that novices miss)

outputs.name: heuristic-library
outputs.desc: The rules of thumb the expert uses, stated as 'when I see X, it usually means Y, so I do Z'

process: Across all cases, list every cue the expert mentioned noticing. A cue is a specific observable thing: a number, a pattern, a behavior, a tone, an absence. Novices do not notice these because they have not learned which signals matter.

For each cue, record what it meant to the expert. The same cue can mean different things to a novice and an expert. A slight hesitation in a patient's voice might mean nothing to a novice but signal hidden symptoms to an experienced clinician.

Extract the heuristics: the expert's rules of thumb. These are usually in the form 'when I see [cue pattern], it usually means [interpretation], so I [action].' The expert may not state them this cleanly; you may need to reconstruct them from the cases.
Verify each heuristic by checking whether it appears in more than one case. A heuristic used in 3 of 5 cases is a core part of the expert's toolkit.

steps.description: Document the extracted knowledge in a format that can be studied and practiced by the learner.

outputs.name: expertise-document
outputs.desc: A structured document containing: the cue catalog, the heuristic library, and 3-5 annotated cases showing the heuristics in action

outputs.name: practice-scenarios
outputs.desc: 5 new scenarios (not from the interview) where the learner can practice applying the heuristics and check their answers against the expert's likely decision

process: Organize the cue catalog by frequency: the cues that appeared in the most cases go first. These are the most important things to learn to notice.
State each heuristic as a decision rule: 'When [specific cue pattern], then [specific action], because [reasoning].' Include the reasoning so the learner can adapt the heuristic to new situations.
Annotate 3 of the original cases with margin notes showing which cue triggered which heuristic at each decision point. This shows the expertise in action.
Create 5 new practice scenarios that require applying the heuristics. Include the 'expert answer' for each, verified with the expert if possible.

steps.description: Have the learner practice on real or simulated cases with the expert observing and correcting in real time.

outputs.name: practice-results
outputs.desc: For each practice case: what the learner decided, what the expert would have decided, and where they diverged

outputs.name: calibration-notes
outputs.desc: Where the learner's application of the heuristics needs adjustment (too aggressive, too conservative, missing a cue, misinterpreting a cue)

process: Present the learner with each practice scenario. Have them talk through their thinking aloud: what cues they notice, what those cues mean, what they would do.
Compare to the expert's expected decision. Where they diverge, identify whether the learner missed a cue, misinterpreted a cue, or applied the wrong heuristic.
Have the expert observe 1-2 real cases where the learner makes the decision and the expert provides feedback immediately after. Real cases reveal gaps that practice scenarios miss.
Repeat until the learner's decisions match the expert's on 80% or more of the decision points. The remaining 20% represents judgment that requires more experience to develop.

description: Break through a skill plateau using three interventions: increase difficulty through constraints, decompose and find the avoided sub-skill, and study someone one level above to identify the specific difference.

steps.description: Confirm you are actually on a plateau (not just in a normal dip) and identify when the plateau started.

inputs.name: skill-description
inputs.desc: The skill where you feel stuck

inputs.name: performance-history
inputs.desc: Evidence of your performance over time (scores, output quality, speed, feedback)

outputs.name: plateau-confirmation
outputs.desc: Whether this is a true plateau (no measurable improvement for 4+ weeks despite regular practice) or a normal fluctuation

outputs.name: plateau-onset
outputs.desc: When the plateau started and what your practice looked like just before it started

process: Plot your performance over time using whatever metric you have. A plateau is a flat line for 4 or more weeks. A dip is a temporary decline followed by improvement. If you have fewer than 4 weeks of flat performance, you may not be on a plateau.
Check that you have actually been practicing during the flat period. No practice means no plateau; it means absence.

Identify the date the plateau started. What were you doing just before? Often a plateau starts right after a period of rapid improvement, because you reached the limit of your current practice method.

Rate your practice quality during the plateau: are you still doing focused, effortful practice, or has practice become comfortable repetition? Comfortable repetition is the most common cause of plateaus.

steps.description: Increase the difficulty of practice by adding constraints that force you out of your comfort zone.

inputs.name: plateau-confirmation
inputs.desc: Confirmation that this is a real plateau

outputs.name: constraint-options
outputs.desc: 3-5 constraints you can add to your practice to increase difficulty (time pressure, resource limits, additional requirements)

outputs.name: selected-constraint
outputs.desc: The constraint that is most likely to push you past the plateau, with the rationale

process: List 3-5 constraints you can add. For a musician: play the piece 20% faster. For a writer: write the same quality in half the word count. For a coder: solve the problem without using a specific library. For a speaker: present with no notes.
The right constraint makes your current approach fail, forcing you to develop a new, better approach. If the constraint does not make you uncomfortable, it is not a real constraint.
Select the constraint that targets the specific part of your practice that has become automatic. The automatic part is where you stopped improving because you stopped thinking.
Apply the constraint for 2 weeks. If your performance drops initially, that is expected. The constraint is exposing a weakness that was hidden by your comfortable routine.

steps.description: Decompose the skill and find the sub-skill you have been unconsciously avoiding because it is difficult or uncomfortable.

outputs.name: sub-skill-decomposition
outputs.desc: The skill broken into 5-8 sub-skills with honest assessment of how much time you spend practicing each

outputs.name: avoided-sub-skill
outputs.desc: The sub-skill you spend the least time on relative to its importance, which is likely the one holding back your overall performance

process: Break the skill into 5-8 sub-skills. For each, estimate what percentage of your practice time goes to it.

Identify the sub-skill that is both important and under-practiced. This is usually the one you avoid because it is frustrating, boring, or embarrassing. You gravitate toward the parts you are already good at because they feel productive.
Verify by asking: if someone watched your practice sessions for a week, what would they say you avoid? The answer is your avoided sub-skill.
The avoided sub-skill is almost always the bottleneck. Improving it by 20% often produces more overall improvement than improving your best sub-skill by 50%.

steps.description: Study someone who is one level above you (not a master, just slightly better) and identify the specific thing they do differently.

inputs.name: avoided-sub-skill
inputs.desc: The sub-skill most likely holding you back

outputs.name: comparison-target
outputs.desc: A specific person who is one level above you in this skill, with evidence of their performance

outputs.name: specific-difference
outputs.desc: The 1-2 specific, observable things they do differently from you that account for the performance gap

process: Find someone who is one level above you, not a world expert. The gap between you and someone one level up is small enough to analyze. The gap between you and a master is too large to be useful.
Observe them performing the skill. Watch recordings if available. Focus on the specific moments where their performance diverges from yours.

Identify 1-2 specific, observable differences. Not vague ('they are more confident') but specific ('they pause for 2 seconds before answering tough questions' or 'they check edge cases before writing the main logic').
The specific difference is your next practice target. You now know exactly what to change, not just 'get better.'

steps.description: Design a drill that combines the constraint, the avoided sub-skill, and the specific difference into one practice exercise.

inputs.name: specific-difference
inputs.desc: The observable difference from the one-level-up study

outputs.name: combined-drill
outputs.desc: A practice exercise that addresses all three plateau factors: adds the constraint, isolates the avoided sub-skill, and implements the specific difference

outputs.name: drill-schedule
outputs.desc: How often to do the drill (3-5 times per week for 3 weeks) and how to measure whether the plateau is breaking

process: Design one drill that hits all three: it forces you to practice the avoided sub-skill, under the added constraint, while implementing the specific difference you observed. This concentrated drill attacks the plateau from three angles simultaneously.
The drill should be 15-30 minutes. Short enough to maintain focus, long enough to get meaningful reps.
Measure your performance at the start of the 3-week drill period using the same metric you used to diagnose the plateau. Re-measure weekly.

If performance improves by the end of week 3, the plateau is breaking. Continue the drill until performance reaches a new stable level, then return to normal practice incorporating the changes. If performance has not improved, one of the three diagnoses was wrong. Revisit the analysis.
